# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why3: I know exactly what my wearers gain over phone captions and asking for repeats, from the testimonials and my own origin story, so I can answer from what I know.

screens.why5: What I typed, 'More of the talk followed without asking for repeats', sits in the box as I wrote it, and nothing here reaches a stranger.
screens.why7: The box meets the card's founder shape: 1 to 4 benefits, at most 9 words each, framed against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the only escape; my single 8-word benefit is a noun phrase naming what changes.

screens.why1: Right after I said what AirCaps does better than today's way, Keel showing back my benefit and the belief it will test is the obvious next check.
screens.why2: 'More of the talk followed' is a stiff, passive way to say it, and in the belief it reads 'would have given them more of the talk followed', which takes a second read even for me.
screens.why3: Missing chunks of a group conversation and having to ask people to repeat is exactly what my wearers, and my co-founder, live every week.
screens.why4: One row, under 9 words, one gain, no overlap, and the 1-to-4 guidance and add/remove controls let me add the eye-contact gain if I want it.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed, 'following more without asking anyone to repeat', only reworded.
screens.why7: My leading benefit is a single noun-phrase row, the belief carries it against the study's hard case ('the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people') rather than any last occasion, and the bar counts no difference or worse against it, so it can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Following more of the talk without asking for repeats' + 'Keeping eye contact instead of reading a phone'; belief: 'For most, with it, the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, they would have followed more of the talk without asking for repeats.'

screens.why1: Once I've said what it does better, the obvious next question is what my wearers have to take on to start using it, before the commercial step.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is how I already talk about onboarding, and the limit of four rows of nine words each is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a new AirCaps wearer does: pair the glasses, put them on in conversations, and keep them charged, so I can answer this from my own product and customers.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with one escape, and 'I'm not sure' fits because it lets a founder leave the dimension out rather than invent an effort.
screens.why5: My two efforts, 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day', stand as I typed them, and nothing of Keel's rewording has crept in yet.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves, base-form, in one voice, under 9 words, two of at most four. Neither repeats Compatibility (phone online) or Purchase friction. The new habit of use is the first row, so the belief can be answered either way.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what they'll have to do to start, Keel shows the efforts it drafted from my answer so I can check them before picking one to test, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Both rows are plain words I'd use with my own customers, though the intro stutters by repeating the title 'What they'll have to do' before the instruction.
screens.why3: Putting the glasses on in a conversation and charging them each day are things my wearers do themselves and would know whether they'd do.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and true to the product, but the one-time step every new wearer hits before first use is missing: installing the app and pairing the glasses to the phone.
screens.why5: 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' keeps what I saved, and the daily charge is a real habit of my product, not a drift from it.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort the wearer takes themselves, in base-form verbs with no 'your', under 9 words; there are 2 rows, which is within 1 to 4; and neither repeats Compatibility (phone online) or Purchase friction, so a Yes or No on either one can support or refute the belief.
screens.instead: Rows: Wear the caption glasses in conversations · Charge the glasses every day · Install the app and pair the glasses once (intro without the repeated title).

screens.why1: Right after I listed what they have to do to start, it makes sense to pick the one effort most likely to stop a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult from using AirCaps.
screens.why2: Wearing caption glasses in conversations and charging them every day are plain words I use myself with customers.
screens.why3: Both are things my wearers would do themselves every week, so they can answer from their own lives.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one a habit of use and one a daily chore, both in my words, with nothing nonsensical or overlapping.
screens.why5: The rows and the belief keep what I typed word for word, and nothing on the screen leaks roles or internals to a stranger.
screens.why7: Each row is a single base-form step the wearer takes themselves, in their voice, with no sign-off, compatibility or purchase ground; the picked row becomes a belief strangers can support or refute on the Yes, Only if, Probably not, No scale, with I can't tell as the escape.

screens.why1: Just before strangers see the study, asking whether to collect emails from people willing to try the glasses is the natural last setup step for me, with a 15-day free-return pair ready to hand out.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with the hint quoting the exact line respondents will see is plain to a founder, and pilot is my trade's word.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers to try the glasses is my own decision, answerable from what I know about my launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks into the respondent's line, which says only 'try this for real', and my pick of Yes is kept.

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer belongs just before launch, but a voice-first video interviewer is an awkward lead for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents, and the screen never acknowledges that.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, though '400 credits' has no dollar meaning and I would read it twice.
screens.why3: Choosing who fronts my study is my call, and I can judge it from the previews.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct, but for my audience the missing choices are a captions-first or text-only interviewer and an ASL-signing one, which matter more than which voice speaks.
screens.why5: It names my respondents correctly and leaks nothing of the glasses or the roles.
screens.instead: How should the interviewer appear to deaf or hard-of-hearing adults? Captions first, with voice off by default / Voice and captions together (Daphne or Saskia) / Signed in ASL with captions.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer is the natural next step after choosing who asks, just before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Daphne, read and tap, and speak or type are all plain words to me, and each option explains itself in one line.
screens.why3: I know my wearers: most read easily and many speak, and some find voice-led video hard, so I can pick from what I know about them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the field, but Daphne is framed as asking 'aloud', which is an odd lead for a deaf audience, and no option lets someone answer in ASL, which some of my sign-first respondents would need.
screens.why5: My pick, Read and tap, is shown as typed, and nothing about the glasses or the wearer role leaks into the options.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? -- Read and tap (they read each question and tap, typing where there is a box) / AI interviewer Daphne (every question captioned on screen, also spoken; answer by typing, tapping or talking) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how people answer, who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The first and third options read plainly, but 'From a search on the Contacts page. Pick a list' leans on a Keel page I haven't been shown anywhere in this flow.
screens.why3: I know who I'll send this to: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know from TranscribeGlass days and the testimonial folks, by name.
screens.why4: The three routes, named people, a found list and one open link posted in a community group, are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach DHH adults, with my pick, people I know by name, among them.
screens.why5: My pick is kept as typed, and nothing about the glasses or the wearer role leaks into this sending screen.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a list I search for in Keel (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title with "3 beliefs: 3 holding", and each card gives its deciding number (6 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6) right beside its status word.
screens.why_b2: Each card plainly says what was counted (said yes, would have gone better, would do it), over how many (6), and where the bar sits (4 of 6); the kicker's 7 answered versus 6 counted is visible even though the reason is not.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are recognisably mine, but the solution statement under the title is garbled ("wearing the glasses an app on lightweight glasses shows live captions... and gets back live captions...") and the relative-advantage line is a clumsy restatement of what I typed.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what three held beliefs mean for AirCaps or what to do next; "What it measures" only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and "Holding up" is not inflated, but 6 counted people is a small sample the page never calls small, and it does not say why one of the 7 was not counted.
screens.instead: Say plainly: 'All three solution beliefs held with 6 of the 7 people who answered (one not counted, because...); this is a small group, so the solution looks right for your wedge, and the next thing to test is price, not the glasses', with my statement written as I typed it, e.g. 'live captions of nearby speech shown inside lightweight glasses'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 6 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 4 of 6', so I can see the result and why it cleared.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over the 6 people counted, and the strip puts the marker at 4 of 6 with the bar's rule spelled out, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Could read captions while watching faces' is the compatibility condition I picked, and the card is titled Compatibility as I checked it.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me this condition won't be what stops deaf and hard-of-hearing adults and points me to adoption friction as the next thing to look at.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', but 'is not what will stop them' is firmer than 6 people can carry, and naming adoption friction as what will stop them states something this card doesn't show.
screens.instead: With 6 people, reading captions while watching faces doesn't look like the blocker, though that is a lean, not a call; check Adoption friction below to see whether wearing the glasses is.

screens.why_b1: The verdict Holding up sits right beside 6 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6, so I know it held and which count decided it.
screens.why_b2: The strip makes the bar plain at 4 of 6, but the chart's 'Better · 6 6 a lot · 0 a little' takes a second look, and with no 'no difference / worse · 0' row the against side is only implied.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage, the moment I lost the conversation with hearing people, and 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats' are all my own words.
screens.why_b4: Sending me to Adoption friction for whether they'd wear the glasses is useful, but the screen doesn't say what a unanimous 'a lot better' means for the idea, such as leading with this benefit.
screens.why_b5: The small group and the hypothetical framing are both flagged honestly, but the question as shown calls AirCaps 'an app', not caption glasses, so the 6 of 6 may be backing a phone captioning app rather than what I'm actually selling.
screens.instead: Ask about AirCaps as 'caption glasses that show what people say in your lenses', show the no difference / worse row at 0, and say: unanimous and strong, so lead with this benefit; the real test is whether they'd wear them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 6 would do it · bar 4 of 6', so I know it held and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the answers over 6 counted people (Yes 4, Only if 2, Probably not 0, No 0), and the strip puts the bar marker at 4 of 6 with its 1-in-3 rule, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card says 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations', the step I picked. The asked clause drops 'caption' but is still clearly mine.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to the 2 is below, but Ruth's note is about catching audience questions and Tomás's is about taking the end seat. Neither says what 'look like ordinary glasses' asks of me, so I get no concrete step: frame design, or a loaner pair like Harriet asks for.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called a lean, not a call, but 'What would make it worth it to those 2 is below' points at quotes that don't answer that, a soft overstatement of what the screen holds.
screens.instead: 4 of 6 would wear them as they are; 2 only if they look like ordinary glasses, so the frames' look is the catch to test (show those 2 the frames, or lend a pair as Harriet asks), and with 6 counted this is a lean.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 6 would do it · bar 4 of 6', and the line 'Adoption friction held, 6 of 6' ties the number to the verdict.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the dimension and belief I checked, in the wording from revision 24.
screens.why_b4: The screen only says 'what they added'. It never says what the two conditions mean for the launch, such as offering a try-before-you-buy or improving audience mic pickup.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the uncounted quote is set apart, but the truncated theme 'Only if they look like ordinary glasses for' sits on all three quotes and states a condition about looks that none of them voices.
screens.why_b6: Ruth's audience-questions pickup and Harriet's borrow-a-pair-under-stage-lights trial are new to me, but Tomás's quote is a current workaround rather than a condition, and the broken theme label is noise.
screens.instead: Held 6 of 6 (bar 4); the 2 conditions are pickup beyond the front speaker in big halls and a way to try the lens under stage lights before buying, so consider a trial pair or venue demo and test far-field audience capture.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check I talk with hearing people before asking how those conversations go.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is the phrase I and other deaf people use every day, so I understand it at once.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and with family every week, so I know the answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers a gate question completely, and the gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it drops 'face to face' and asks about a habit ('every week') rather than the last 7 days, so it lets in texting or a signed relay call and drifts a little.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky for a yes/no gate where 'Yes or no.' would say it plainly.
screens.instead: In the last week, did you talk face to face with hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those talks went wrong for me this past week.
screens.why2: I'd say I 'lost track of' or 'couldn't follow' the conversation; 'lose the conversation' reads oddly, a bit like losing an argument, so I'd take a second to be sure what it means.
screens.why3: Whether I fell behind at a dinner, a shop counter or a meeting this week is exactly what I know from my own week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it and both are true of someone, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: It asks about failing to follow the talk, which is the problem itself, and nothing about any product, app or captioning idea reaches me.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no' is easy to catch once, though if I'm relying on captions of the AI voice, 'lose the conversation' is the one phrase I'd want said more plainly.
screens.why7: It is two fixed answers on the founder's problem rather than the routine: someone whose only talks this week were quiet one-on-ones with people they lip-read well could truly say No, and I'd say Yes, so the share can hold or fail.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: After I said whether I lost the thread with hearing people this week, showing me the idea before part 2 makes sense.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and the lens are words I already use, and I'd follow it on first reading.
screens.why3: Reading captions while trying to keep my eyes on the person talking is exactly what I juggle every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is an idea card shown on purpose, and the belief about reading words while keeping eye contact is said plainly, with no internal terms for people like me.
screens.why6: It says well enough, but the second sentence repeats 'lightweight glasses with an app' from the first, so it drags when heard.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions of nearby speech. When people near you talk, their words appear inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, it makes sense to ask whether I could follow captions and still watch people's faces, which is what I rely on.
screens.why2: Captions, faces and conversation are my everyday words; I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I had no captions in front of me at my last conversation, so I'd be picturing whether my eyes could manage both, a fair guess but still a guess, and I might just answer No because there were no captions.
screens.why4: The four steps from easily to no cover how it goes for me, they don't overlap, and I can't tell fits.
screens.why5: Captions came from the idea card, and nothing about the company or its own terms for me crept in.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options I can hold, one escape at the end; it says well.
screens.why7: It is an ability on one measure, with the ability four in order and I can't tell apart; it tests the step the glasses depend on, and some of us could do it while others couldn't, so it can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. If captions had been in front of your eyes, could you have read them while watching faces? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions question, it makes sense to ask whether the glasses would have helped the last time I lost the conversation.
screens.why2: "Would AirCaps have done that better" reads as if it would have lost the conversation better; I had to read it twice to understand it means following the conversation better.
screens.why3: I lose conversations with hearing people most weeks, so I can picture the last time and judge whether captions on my glasses would have helped.
screens.why4: The four answers cover the range from a lot better to worse without overlapping, and I can't tell fits as the way out.
screens.why5: "AirCaps, an app" leaves out the glasses, which is the part that matters to me because I want to keep watching faces, so it drifted a little from the card above.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options and the escape said last, so I can hold it in my head, read on the captions or on the screen.
screens.why7: The four answers, their order, the two for and two against, and the escape apart all meet the card, but "done that better" leaves unclear what is being made better, which is the card's own pitfall.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation with hearing people. Would AirCaps, captions on your glasses, have helped you follow it, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After hearing about captions on glasses and whether it would help, asking whether I'd actually wear them in my conversations is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Wear the glasses in your conversations is plain to me, and the condition about looking like ordinary glasses is exactly how I'd say it.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd put glasses on when talking with hearing people at work, the shop or with family -- it's my own face and my own conversations.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition, probably not, no and I can't tell cover it, and the condition is the one most of us would actually raise.
screens.why5: The card names AirCaps and the glasses on purpose, and the question uses no inside words about me -- just my conversations.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold when spoken, the escape said last.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses is a step I take myself, the options run yes, my own condition, probably not, no in order with I can't tell apart, and the belief can be held up or knocked down.

screens.why1: After three questions about the idea, asking what would make it worth it to me is the natural last thing to ask before I go.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and AirCaps is the name I was just given, so I can answer on first reading or hearing without working anything out.
screens.why3: I know what I need when I lose a conversation at dinner or at the counter, like captions fast enough to keep up, accurate in noise, and glasses I'd actually wear, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It keeps to the AirCaps idea I was shown and adds none of the founder's own terms or plans.
screens.why6: One short question said in one breath, with no list, symbol or aside to hold.
screens.instead: What would make wearing AirCaps in your conversations clearly worth it to you?
